analogy.p: Macduff is like a lighthouse keeper who stays away from home to keep the light burning; the storm (Macbeth's tyranny) wrecks the cottage he leaves behind. He saves the ships but loses his family, which makes his victory costly. The analogy shows both his duty and his guilt. It breaks down because the lighthouse keeper did not know the storm would hit his own home, while Macduff leaves with the knowledge that Macbeth is a tyrant.

bullets: **Macduff** is the instrument of providential justice: the tyrant is killed by a man born “untimely ripped”, a sign that the natural order is reasserting itself.
**He is a foil** to Macbeth: where Macbeth suppresses feeling, Macduff insists on grieving; where Macbeth fears the future, Macduff acts to restore it.
**Lady Macduff** represents domestic love, motherhood and innocence, in contrast to Lady Macbeth, who rejects maternal values.
**Their son** shows the loss of the future generation, which the play values as continuity (compare Fleance and Malcolm).

callouts.p: A character whose main dramatic function is to take revenge on behalf of a wronged person or order. Macduff avenges Duncan, his own family and Scotland.

Macduff's revenge is presented as justified, yet it is also personal: “My wife and children's ghosts will haunt me still”. The best answers explain how Shakespeare blends moral duty with private grief.

core.h: Dramatic function: avenger, foil and conscience
core.p: Macduff is the Thane of Fife whose actions drive the play's resolution. He is the first to discover Duncan's body, the first to refuse to attend Macbeth's coronation, the leader of the English forces beside Malcolm, and the man who kills Macbeth. Lady Macduff and her son are the victims who give his revenge moral weight. Together they present the family life that Macbeth destroys and which stands as the alternative to the Macbeth marriage.

bullets: The **triple repetition** “horror, horror, horror” and the sense that language fails show genuine shock, in contrast to Macbeth's performed grief a moment later.
He rings the alarm bell and calls on the household to wake, bringing the private crime into the public world.
He tells Lady Macbeth “The repetition in a woman's ear / Would murder as it fell”. This is **dramatic irony**: the audience knows she is the one who planned the murder.

In 2.4 he tells Ross that he will not go to the coronation at Scone, and adds “Lest our old robes sit easier than our new!” The clothing metaphor suggests that Macbeth's rule is ill-fitting and that Macduff mistrusts it from the start.

callouts.p: Compare Macduff's spontaneous “O horror” with Macbeth's calculated speech about Duncan's “silver skin laced with his golden blood”. The language of the real horror is simple; the language of performance is ornate.
callouts.t: Use his discovery as a contrast

core.h: Act 2: the discoverer and the first to resist
core.p: Macduff appears in 2.3 at the knocking at the gate. He arrives early to wake the king, which makes him the person who finds the body. His horrified outburst, “O horror, horror, horror!” and “Tongue nor heart / Cannot conceive nor name thee”, pushes language to its limit, while “Confusion now hath made his masterpiece” and the reference to “the Lord's anointed temple” show that he reads the murder as a sacrilege against the order of nature and God.

bullets: The apparition's warning shows that Macbeth's fear is not unfounded: Macduff is the one who will end him.
Macbeth's decision to “give to th' edge o' th' sword / His wife, his babes” is a moral low point: he turns from killing rivals to killing the innocent.
The scene is structurally significant: the tyrant's determination to act “from this moment” leads straight into 4.2.
Macduff's decision to leave his family is the source of the play's most difficult question: is he a loyal patriot or an irresponsible husband?
core.h: Act 3 and the move to England
core.p: Macduff is absent from the stage for much of Act 3 and Act 4, which makes his absence a source of tension. Macbeth notes in 3.4 that Macduff “denies his person / At our great bidding”, and in 3.6 Lennox and another lord reveal that Macduff has gone to England to join Malcolm. The audience sees the political resistance gathering offstage while the tyrant grows paranoid. In 4.1 the witches warn Macbeth to “Beware Macduff”, and Macbeth, in a reckless turn, decides to take revenge on his family.

bullets: She and her son are shown in domestic intimacy: their playful dialogue (“As birds do, mother”) makes the child lively and clever.
Her pessimistic reflection “where to do harm / Is often laudable” is a **moral judgement on the age**: in a tyranny, goodness is a danger.
The child's question “Was my father a traitor, mother?” and the discussion of what a traitor is introduces the idea that **language can be twisted**, linking to “Fair is foul”.

When the murderers arrive, the son says “Thou liest, thou shag-haired villain!” and dies with the words “He has killed me, mother: / Run away, I pray you!” He dies protecting her, and his courage shows what Macbeth has destroyed.
The scene is **short, fast and violent** after a long build-up of tenderness. The contrast intensifies the horror.

callouts.p: 4.2 is where the audience's sympathy for Macbeth is exhausted. It marks the point at which the play's sense of justice moves from the political (a usurper) to the moral (a murderer of children).
callouts.t: Do not dismiss the scene as filler

core.h: Act 4 Scene 2: Lady Macduff and her son
core.p: This scene is the emotional centre of the second half. Lady Macduff is introduced as a loving mother angry at her husband for fleeing. She says “He loves us not; / He wants the natural touch”, and compares him unfavourably to “the poor wren, / The most diminutive of birds”, which will “fight, / Her young ones in her nest, against the owl”. The image of the tiny bird defending its nest contrasts with the powerful man who has left his children.

bullets: Both women are limited by the roles available to them, but their responses are opposite.
Lady Macduff's anger at her husband makes her human and avoids the stereotype of the silent victim.
The word “traitor” is applied to Macduff by his own wife in the scene, to show confusion and fear in an unjust regime.

callouts.p: Use Lady Macduff in answers about gender, family or the consequences of tyranny: she is the innocent counterpart of Lady Macbeth and a measure of Macbeth's moral collapse.

core.h: Lady Macduff compared with Lady Macbeth
core.p: Shakespeare sets the two wives side by side to explore what it means to be a wife, a mother and a woman in power. Lady Macbeth calls on spirits to “unsex” her and boasts about how she would dash out a baby's brains if she had sworn to do so. Lady Macduff protects her child, fears for him, and is killed because of her husband's politics. The contrast shows two models of womanhood that the play evaluates.

Lady Macbeth
Lady Macduff

Seeks power through her husband and crime
Has no political power; victim of it
Murdered on stage; remembered with pity

bullets: Macduff's phrase “He has no children” can refer to Macbeth (so he cannot understand the loss) or to Malcolm (who tells him to be strong); critics debate this, so offer both readings.
The image of “pretty chickens and their dam / At one fell swoop” compares the family to birds killed by a hawk, echoing Lady Macduff's wren image.
His self-blame, “Sinful Macduff, / They were all struck for thee”, adds guilt to grief and humanises him.
His vow to meet Macbeth “front to front” and leave him “within my sword's length” turns private sorrow into political action.
The scene redefines **manhood**: for Malcolm it means controlled revenge; for Macduff it means feeling deeply and then acting.

callouts.p: The play contrasts Macbeth's idea that manhood is ruthless violence with Macduff's idea that manhood includes grief. Both men kill, but Macduff's revenge is guided by feeling and duty, not by fear.

core.h: Act 4 Scene 3: grief, manhood and revenge
core.p: In England, Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty by pretending to be a worse tyrant than Macbeth. Macduff reacts with horror to the idea that such a man could rule, saying “Fit to govern? / No, not to live”. The scene then turns when Ross brings the news of the massacre. Macduff's first reaction is disbelief and a repeated question: “All my pretty ones? / Did you say all? O hell-kite! All?” The repetition shows him struggling to take in the scale of loss. When Malcolm tells him to “Dispute it like a man”, he replies “But I must also feel it as a man.”

bullets: Macduff's “Turn, hell-hound, turn!” casts Macbeth as a devilish creature, a language of damnation which fits the Jacobean idea of evil.
“I have no words; / My voice is in my sword” shows the same emotional simplicity that marked his reaction at the discovery of Duncan.

The revelation that he was “from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped” makes him the agent of the supernatural wording of the prophecy: it is both a clever twist and a sign of a world turned unnatural.

He re-enters with Macbeth's head and presents it to Malcolm: “Hail, King! for so thou art”, pointing to “Th' usurper's cursed head”. He is the first to salute the new king, which restores political order.
The ending leaves Macduff as the representative of loyalty, feeling and duty, qualities that the play values above ambition.

callouts.p: In 5.8 Macbeth realises that the witches have deceived him (“juggling fiends”), and Macduff's birth is the trigger. This is a good moment to discuss equivocation, free will and Macbeth's anagnorisis.
callouts.t: Link the death to the prophecies

core.h: Acts 5: the avenger and the end of the tyrant
core.p: In 5.7 Macduff searches for Macbeth with the cry “Tyrant, show thy face!” and fears that “My wife and children's ghosts will haunt me still”. The speech shows that his motive is personal, since he fears that if Macbeth dies by another hand, his family will not be avenged. In 5.8, the duel is brief but dense with meaning. Macbeth admits that he has avoided Macduff because his soul is “too much charged / With blood of thine already”, showing that guilt is still alive in him.

bullets: In 4.3 we hear of the English king's healing touch for “the evil”, contrasting a holy king with a tyrant. A Jacobean audience, with a king who also touched for the “King's Evil”, would see a compliment.
Do not argue that Macduff is simply right; offer the possibility that his flight led to the massacre and that his guilt is real.

callouts.p: Some students present Macduff as a flawless hero. The better response notes his ambiguity: he leaves his family undefended, and Lady Macduff's accusation of cowardice sits uneasily alongside Malcolm's praise of his loyalty.

core.p: Macduff and his family can be read in several ways, and Shakespeare's Jacobean audience would bring specific expectations to them. Use contexts to explain why the revenge feels justified, why the massacre is so shocking, and why the play ends in Malcolm's restoration.

head: Context or reading
What it adds
Where to use it
rows: Macduff's killing of a usurper is a restoration of divine order, not a murder
Killing a child was a breach of the deepest natural law; the scene invites pity and moral outrage
A father was responsible for his household; Macduff's absence may be seen as neglect, but also as duty to the country
Audiences expected a revenge plot with a justified avenger; Macduff fits this model while being tied to the supernatural prophecy
Macduff prays to heaven and ends the tyrant; the healing of the nation under Malcolm is a form of providence
4.3 and the English king's healing touch

bullets: **Know the key scenes**: 2.3 (the discovery), 4.2 (the massacre), 4.3 (grief and revenge), 5.8 (the duel).
**Memorise five quotations**: “O horror, horror, horror!”, “He wants the natural touch”, “All my pretty ones?”, “feel it as a man”, “Turn, hell-hound, turn!”.
**Contrast pairs**: Macduff and Macbeth (grief and numbness); Lady Macduff and Lady Macbeth (nurture and rejection).
**Use structure**: the placement of 4.2 just before the English scene shows the cost of tyranny and then the response to it.
**Context as argument**: the audience's view of providence and the king's role helps explain why Macduff's victory is a restoration.

callouts.p: Shakespeare presents Macduff as a man whose capacity for grief, not violence alone, makes him the moral opposite of Macbeth, and whose revenge restores a natural order that the tyrant has violated.

core.h: Exam technique: writing about Macduff and Lady Macduff
core.p: Macduff appears in questions on revenge, loyalty, manhood, family and the resolution of the play. Extract questions often use 2.3, 4.2 or 4.3. In part (b), use him as a contrast to Macbeth or Lady Macbeth to give the argument balance.

5.7 and 5.8: the avenger and the prophecy
Context: providence, revenge tragedy and the restoration of order
essays.q: How does Shakespeare present Macduff as a contrast to Macbeth? (Part (b) style)
essays.text:
Shakespeare introduces Macduff in 2.3 as the man who first discovers the crime, and his language marks him out from Macbeth immediately. His “O horror, horror, horror!” is a triple repetition in which language collapses in the face of regicide; it is the voice of a man who cannot find words because he feels too much. Macbeth, by contrast, produces ornate metaphors about “silver skin laced with his golden blood”, a polished performance that shows the gap between true and false grief. The contrast is also structural, because Macduff's direct, unembellished response follows the dagger and the murder and so represents the reaction of an ordinary human conscience to a crime against God's order.

The scene in 4.2 deepens the contrast by showing what Macduff's absence costs. Lady Macduff accuses him that “He wants the natural touch”, and her image of the “poor wren”, fighting an owl to protect its young, makes his flight to England seem a failure of instinct. The audience, however, knows from 4.1 that Macbeth has ordered the massacre, so her words are charged with dramatic irony. The wit of the child (“As birds do, mother”) makes his death more painful, and his final words “He has killed me, mother: / Run away, I pray you!” show a courage that exposes the cowardice of the tyrant's order. The scene suggests that Macduff's guilt is real but that the greater guilt lies with the man who makes goodness “dangerous folly”.

In 4.3 Shakespeare allows Macduff to articulate a different idea of manhood. Malcolm says “Dispute it like a man”, the same kind of language that Lady Macbeth used to goad her husband; Macduff replies “But I must also feel it as a man.” The addition “also” is quiet but profound: Macduff refuses to accept that courage must replace feeling. The repeated “All my pretty ones?” shows his difficulty in accepting the loss, and the tender adjective “pretty” belongs to the world of the nursery, not the battlefield. Where Macbeth, in 5.5, receives news of his wife's death with “She should have died hereafter”, numb and empty, Macduff turns grief into a purpose. This is the central moral contrast of the play: suffering either deadens or motivates.

By Act 5 the contrast has become a duel. Macduff's “Tyrant, show thy face!” shows that he fears his family's ghosts if someone else kills Macbeth, so his violence is personal and moral. In 5.8 his “Turn, hell-hound, turn!” casts Macbeth as a devilish animal, a figure for a Jacobean audience of damnation. The revelation that Macduff was “untimely ripped” makes him the instrument of a providential order that works through a twist of nature. When he re-enters with Macbeth's head and proclaims “Hail, King!”, the restoration of order is complete.

Shakespeare's purpose is therefore to show that ambition without feeling destroys the self, while feeling with duty can renew a nation. The contrast also leaves a final complexity: Macduff's victory is real but is bought with the lives of those he left behind, so the restoration of order carries the memory of its cost.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents Macduff as Macbeth's moral opposite: where Macbeth suppresses feeling and fears the future, Macduff insists on grief and acts to restore the natural order, so that the victory of the avenger is the victory of feeling over ambition.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (feeling versus ambition) organises the argument; quotations are short and embedded.
AO2: considers repetition, diminutive imagery (“pretty”, “wren”), dramatic irony, antithesis and structure (placing 4.2 before 4.3).
AO3: context (providence, revenge tragedy, Jacobean ideas of manhood and kingship) supports the interpretation of the ending.
Weighs Macduff's guilt against his heroism and evaluates Shakespeare's purpose in the conclusion.

exam.q: Starting with this extract (Act 4 Scene 2, Lady Macduff and her son), explain how Shakespeare presents the effects of Macbeth's tyranny on innocent people. (Part (a) style; check the marks on your paper, around 20.)
exam.tip: Keep your analysis on language and staging in the extract and link to the idea of tyranny.

2.4: refuses to attend the coronation; clothing imagery
4.3: “feel it as a man” versus ruthless manhood
Reaction to loss: Macduff grieves, Macbeth is numb

Context: restoration of order under Malcolm

exam.tip: Use a contrast structure: “whereas Macbeth..., Macduff...”.

exam.tip: One clear difference with evidence and an explanation of what it shows.

exam.tip: The strongest answers take a firm view but explore the ambiguity of Macduff's decision.

mistakes.r: Discuss his ambiguity: duty to Scotland versus abandonment of his family; he says “Sinful Macduff”.
Analyse her anger (“He wants the natural touch”), her philosophy (“to do good sometime / Accounted dangerous folly”) and her role as foil to Lady Macbeth.
mistakes.w: Treating Lady Macduff as a minor victim with no personality.

mistakes.r: Zoom in on a phrase, such as “shag-haired villain” or “He has killed me, mother”, and explain how the scene builds tension and pathos.
Discuss the placing of the massacre before the English scene: tyranny's cost, then the response.
Link revenge tragedy conventions and providence to Macduff's lines in 5.7 and 5.8.
mistakes.w: Context without a link: “Jacobean people liked revenge”.

mistakes.r: Offer both readings (Macbeth or Malcolm) and say what each suggests.
mistakes.w: Saying “He has no children” definitely refers to Macbeth.

mistakes.r: Contrast Malcolm's “Dispute it like a man” with Macduff's “feel it as a man” and link to Macbeth's earlier definition of manhood.

quotes.a: The triple repetition shows that language fails in the face of the crime, giving the sense of a genuine, spontaneous reaction. The abstract noun “horror” is more powerful than any description. It contrasts with Macbeth's formal grief that follows, which is polished and artificial.
quotes.c: The murder of a king was a sacrilege, so his reaction reflects the Jacobean understanding of regicide as an offence against God.

quotes.a: “Confusion” personifies chaos as an artist who has produced his greatest work. The word “masterpiece” is darkly ironic because it dignifies a murder by treating it as creative. The line also shows Macduff as a man who sees the murder as a sign that the whole order of things has collapsed.
quotes.c: In the Great Chain of Being, killing a king caused disorder in the whole world.
quotes.q: Confusion now hath made his masterpiece
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 3, early in the scene

quotes.a: Macduff protects Lady Macbeth from the news, assuming a woman's ear is too delicate. This produces strong dramatic irony because she is the one who planned it. The line also shows the period's assumptions about gender, which she has rejected.
quotes.c: Jacobean views of women as gentle and sheltered are being used ironically against the play's most ruthless woman.
quotes.q: The repetition in a woman's ear
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 3, Macduff to Lady Macbeth

quotes.a: She judges her husband as lacking natural parental affection, and uses the word “wants” in the sense of “lacks”. The phrase suggests that family bonds are a part of nature, so Macduff's absence is both emotional and moral. Her anger reveals her fear and love.
quotes.c: A father was expected to protect his household; her words reflect the patriarchal expectations of the period.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 2, Lady Macduff to Ross

quotes.a: The wren is one of the smallest birds, yet it fights an owl to protect its young. The comparison shows how far Macduff falls short of natural instincts, and the epithet “poor” gives the bird pity and dignity. It also foreshadows the destruction of her own nest.
quotes.c: Owls were associated with death and ill omens, adding to the sense of danger.

quotes.a: In a world ruled by a tyrant, harm is “laudable” and goodness is a risk. This moral inversion echoes “Fair is foul, and foul is fair”. The adverb “sometime” suggests that goodness is rare, and the word “folly” shows how power makes virtue look stupid.
quotes.c: Jacobean audiences feared tyranny and the breakdown of moral order that might follow a usurper.
quotes.q: to do good sometime / Accounted dangerous folly
quotes.t: Moral inversion, antithesis, echo of the witches

quotes.a: The simple statement, followed by “Run away, I pray you!”, presents the child as brave and unselfish. The monosyllables make the line direct and heartbreaking. It is the moral low point of the play because innocence is destroyed by a regime.
quotes.c: The slaughter of children recalled biblical massacres and was seen as the worst crime.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 2, the son's last words

quotes.a: The question and repetition (“Did you say all?”) show that he cannot take in the scale of loss. The word “pretty” is tender and domestic, contrasting with the violence. The following image of “chickens and their dam” shows the family as helpless creatures killed by a hawk.
quotes.c: The play stresses the family as a model of natural order, which the tyrant destroys.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 3, Macduff on hearing the news

quotes.a: Macduff redefines manhood as the capacity to feel, rejecting Malcolm's advice to dispute grief. The phrase contrasts directly with Lady Macbeth's equation of manhood with ruthlessness. It also gives his later revenge moral weight because it is rooted in love and not ambition.
quotes.c: The Jacobean ideal of masculinity combined courage with feeling; the play tests that ideal.

quotes.a: The imperative and monosyllables create a fierce, urgent rhythm. “Hell-hound” presents Macbeth as a devilish animal, hunted and cornered. The language of the hunt reverses the earlier situation where the tyrant hunted others.
quotes.c: Hell and damnation were central to the Jacobean moral imagination, so the label would be highly charged.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 8, early in the scene

quotes.a: The phrase describes a caesarean birth, which makes Macduff technically not “of woman born”. The harsh verb “ripped” is violent and unnatural, in tune with a play in which nature is disordered. The twist shows that the witches' prophecies are riddles.
quotes.c: The revelation shows the power of equivocation, which was a live issue after the Gunpowder Plot trials.

summary: Understand how Macduff acts as the play's avenger and Macbeth's moral opposite, and how Lady Macduff and her son embody family, innocence and the cost of tyranny; know the key scenes (2.3, 4.2, 4.3, 5.7, 5.8), the language, and the contexts that give them meaning.

terms.d: A character whose role is to take revenge for a wrong; Macduff avenges Duncan and his family.
A character who contrasts with another, such as Macduff against Macbeth.
When the audience knows more than the characters, as in 4.2 where we know the murderers are coming.
A quality that evokes pity or sorrow, as in the scene of Lady Macduff's son.
Ambiguous language that misleads; the prophecy “none of woman born” is an example.
The belief that God guides events; Macduff is seen as the instrument of providence.
A social system in which men hold power and women are subordinate; relevant to the roles of both Ladies.
A ruler who governs through fear and violence, as Macbeth does.
Language that creates pictures in the mind, such as birds and nests in 4.2 and 4.3.
Placing contrasting scenes or ideas side by side, e.g. domestic life in 4.2 and murder in the same scene.
